derivation.note: Which namespaces are derived deterministically from structured vendor strings and which are model judgements. Only judgement namespaces reach the risk path. The workload namespace is both: the seven tags in derived_from_title_component are asserted deterministically from the component half of the MSRC title, and the assessor may add to that set but never subtract from it. Leaving these to judgement alone cost 20 of 27 Remote Desktop records and 11 of 26 identity records their filter tag on 2026-Sep.

definitions._note: Judgement tags gate mitigation credit and risk archetypes, so what they mean cannot be left to the reader. Added 2026-09-11 after an adversarial review rejected 30.9% of delivery tags - almost entirely because the scorer read 'user-content' in the web-application sense (content authored by users) while the assessor used the patch-triage sense (attacker content a user must open). Both readings were defensible from the name. Neither was written down.
definitions.user-content: Attacker-supplied content that reaches a user and must be opened, previewed or rendered by them - a malicious document, attachment or media file. It does NOT mean content authored by users. This is the sense that email/web filtering and Protected View act on.
definitions.email: The attacker-supplied content plausibly arrives by mail flow, per the vendor's own description or FAQ.
definitions.web: The attacker-supplied content plausibly arrives by web browsing or download, per the vendor's description or FAQ.
definitions.remote-service: The vulnerable code is reached over the network by a service listening for connections, with no user action.
definitions.local-access: Exploitation requires the attacker to already have local access to the host.
definitions._workload_note: Workload definitions are CRITERIA, not membership lists. Added 2026-09-11 after the cycle-6 definitions failed to move workload tags (80.9% -> 81.0%) while delivery moved +17.2 and impact +4.9. The cause was the form of the definition, not its absence: each workload tag was written as a closed enumeration, and the adversarial scorer read the enumeration as a whitelist. 20 of the 25 surviving rejections were on the four tags that HAD a definition, and their rationales reason from the list - 'Remote Desktop Client is not one of the three components the authoritative tag definition covers', 'Microsoft Account is not among the authoritative tag definition's enumerated infrastructure technologies'. The same scorer ruled the same component (Remote Desktop Client) both ways depending on whether it read a list or a rule. Each workload definition therefore states an inclusion RULE, marks its enumeration as illustrative, and carries an explicit boundary clause - the shape that worked for user-content and remote-code-execution. The rule is anchored to the tag's operational job: data/product-filters.json makes several workload tags user-facing checkboxes and engine.js matches records on `tags`, so the question a workload tag answers is 'should an administrator who runs this workload see this record?'. That is why client-side components are in scope where the administrator patches them; it is NOT a licence to admit any product that merely touches the same concept.
definitions.identity: The affected component's own job is establishing, issuing, validating, storing or federating identities, credentials, tickets or certificates. Active Directory Domain Services, domain controllers, Kerberos and the Key Distribution Center, Netlogon, Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS), Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS), Entra ID, Azure AD B2C, Microsoft Account and the Microsoft authentication libraries are examples, not the whole list: a component qualifies by doing that job, not by appearing here. The test is whether an administrator responsible for identity infrastructure needs to see this record. It does NOT mean authentication or authorization inside a product whose primary function is something else - a database's access control, an AI or low-code service's permission model, a mail or collaboration server's own token validation, a browser's credential handling - nor device management, nor name resolution, which carries its own tag.
definitions.web-server: The affected component serves HTTP or HTTPS requests: it is the server side of the web. IIS, Apache httpd, nginx, Erlang inets/httpd, HTTP.sys and HTTP listeners embedded in an application or runtime are examples, not the whole list - a component qualifies by answering requests, not by being named here, and the vendor need not call the host a web server. It does NOT mean HTTP client code, a browser, or a component that merely makes outbound web requests.
definitions.file-services: The affected component shares files over a network, or is the client redirector that consumes such a share: SMB/CIFS, NFS, DFS and Samba are examples, not the whole list. A component qualifies by serving or consuming files over the network. It does NOT mean a local or cluster filesystem implementation - ext4, OCFS2 or GFS2 on-disk structures and their utilities are storage defects, not a file-sharing role - and it does not mean file handling inside an application.
definitions.remote-desktop: The affected component is part of the Microsoft Remote Desktop stack, at either end of the connection: Remote Desktop Services and the session host, the RDP protocol implementation, Remote Desktop Gateway, Connection Broker and Web Access, and the Remote Desktop client and app are examples, not the whole list; a component qualifies by being part of that stack. Client-side components are IN SCOPE. An administrator who runs Remote Desktop must patch the endpoints that connect as well as the hosts that listen, and the Remote Desktop filter exists to show them both; a definition that admitted only the listening side would hide half the estate's exposure. It does NOT mean unrelated remote-access technology from another vendor that merely provides a remote screen or shell, nor generic remote administration.
definitions.remote-code-execution: Arbitrary code execution as the IMPACT CLASS, following the vendor's own title convention. It does not assert network reachability: reachability is carried by the CVSS attack vector, which the risk model reads separately. A record titled 'Remote Code Execution Vulnerability' with AV:L is correctly tagged remote-code-execution; duplicating reachability here would make the tag disagree with the vector field.
definitions.elevation-of-privilege: The impact is gaining privileges the attacker did not hold. Reachability and prerequisites are carried by the CVSS vector, not by this tag.
definitions.information-disclosure: The impact is disclosure of data the attacker should not be able to read.
definitions.denial-of-service: The impact is loss of availability of the affected component or host.
definitions.security-feature-bypass: The impact is circumventing a security control the vendor names, without directly gaining code execution or privileges.
definitions.spoofing: The impact is impersonation of a user, host or origin, or misrepresentation of content provenance.
